title: Ask about goals and motives
statement: Ask inference questions about characters' goals, motives and relationships: they draw out the causal inferences skilled readers make, building story understanding as effectively as a text stating those links.
detail: Lesson research for a reading unit took its inference evidence from a 2008 literature review for Key Stages 2 and 3, quoted directly. The review reports that asking inference questions about relationships between characters, goals and motivations enhanced story understanding as effectively as modifying the story so that all this information was stated (Sundbye 1987, quoted through McGee and Johnson 2003), and that why-questions were particularly beneficial to pupils in years 4 to 8 (Pressley 2000). The research called the first the strongest single result for its design, since a good motive question does as much as rewriting the text to state the answer. The finding reaches the lesson secondhand, through the review.
against: The same review cautions that, although the characteristics of good inferencers have been identified, "there is limited research evidence" on how best to improve pupils' inferencing, and the brief calls its routine well motivated and thinly evidenced as a routine (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l3-circe-and-the-lotus-eaters.md`, lines 347-350). Where such questions go also matters: in another study, frequent causal questions during reading cut grade-4 recall of what they did not ask about (few-questions-during-reading).

evidence.quote: Sundbye found that asking inference questions about "relationships between characters, goals and motivations enhanced story understanding as effectively as if the story had been modified so that all this information were explicitly stated" (Kispal, quoting McGee and Johnson 2003 on Sundbye 1987). That last one is the strongest single result for our design: a good motive question does as much as rewriting the text to state the answer.
Pressley found why-questions "particularly beneficial to pupils in years 4-8"
My primary source is the NFER review of the inference literature for Key Stages 2 and 3 by Kispal, which reviews the primary studies and is quoted below
comprehension is guided by why questions, rather than what-happens-next, how, when or where questions
the answers to why-questions expose superordinate goals and causal antecedents
why-questions "particularly beneficial to pupils in years 4-8"

Although the characteristics of good inferencers have been identified, there is limited research evidence
